lead.text: *Situations from crisis leadership, family life, and moral judgment.*

The main text's Situation Library provided quick first moves for 50 common situations, and 15 full-card treatments. Here are 15 more, focused on domains the main text touched only briefly: crisis leadership, family conflict, moral gray zones, and situations involving power and vulnerability.

entries.title: Card #16: The Public Failure of Your Product

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
Your product has a highly visible failure. Customers are angry on social media. Journalists are calling. Your CEO is asking you what to say.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Draft an over-worded corporate apology. Delay by 24 hours to 'get the response right.' Refuse to talk to specific angry customers directly.
WHY IT FAILS
Corporate-speak is instantly recognizable and reads as evasion. Delay compounds anger. Silence to specific customers is remembered forever by those customers and their networks.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE

Own the specific failure fast, in plain language, with a concrete next action and a timeline. Reach out to the loudest few customers personally. Do the harder internal work of preventing recurrence in parallel.
WORDS TO USE

*"We have a specific problem: [X]. It affected [Y customers, over Z hours]. Here is what happened, in plain terms: [description]. Here is what we're doing about it today, and by when: [specifics]. Here is what we're doing this month to prevent recurrence: [specifics]. If you were affected, please reach out at [specific channel] and I personally will respond within 24 hours."*
*"This shouldn't have happened. I take responsibility."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"We take this issue very seriously and are committed to the highest standards of customer satisfaction."*
*"Our team is working diligently to resolve the matter."*
*"Some customers may have experienced…"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Even honest, fast, specific responses can be insufficient if the underlying failure was genuinely severe. Sometimes the honest response leads to the conclusion that the product cannot continue without a major restructuring. That is also a legitimate response to some failures.

entries.title: Card #17: A Team Member Discloses Something Private

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
A direct report tells you, in a 1:1, that they are dealing with a serious personal situation — an illness, a divorce, a family crisis, mental health struggles. They ask you not to share it.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Nod, express sympathy, treat them the same as before, hope things improve. Or: over-adjust, quietly reduce their workload, treat them as fragile without consulting them.
WHY IT FAILS

Treating them the same misses the fact that they told you FOR A REASON. Silently reducing their workload removes their agency and can feel like demotion. Both responses fail to honor what the disclosure actually meant.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE

Thank them for trusting you. Ask what they specifically need from you — accommodation, silence, permission to take time. Do exactly that. Check in privately, briefly, at a cadence they agree to. Respect the confidence.
WORDS TO USE
*"Thank you for telling me. That took trust and I won't share it beyond you and me."*
*"What would be helpful — accommodation on workload, flexibility on hours, or something else? Or do you want to just have me know and not adjust anything?"*
*"If you want, we can plan a brief check-in each week — even just 5 minutes — and you can tell me then if anything has shifted."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"Whatever you need, we'll figure it out. [without specifics]"*
*"Oh, that must be so hard. My aunt went through something similar…"*
*"Let me know if you need anything. [when a specific offer is warranted]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some legal jurisdictions require disclosure of certain situations (e.g. serious mental health risks affecting workplace safety). If you are unclear about your legal obligations, consult HR — without revealing the specific person unless required. The confidence matters, and so do the legal frames around it.

entries.title: Card #18: You Are Being Managed Out — Quietly

blocks.text: THE SITUATION

You've noticed the signals: fewer meaningful assignments, less visibility, cooler relationships with leadership, vague feedback that doesn't translate to specific improvements. Nobody has said anything, but something has shifted.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Try harder at your current job. Interpret the shift as your fault and work longer hours. Or: complain to peers about the unfairness. Or: pretend it isn't happening.
WHY IT FAILS

Working harder at the wrong thing doesn't help. Complaining to peers becomes visible to leadership and confirms the impression they've been forming. Pretending compounds the eventual moment when things become explicit.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Get the truth. Directly. From your manager. Then plan your response based on the truth — including the possibility that you should be leaving.
WORDS TO USE

*"I want to have a direct conversation with you. I've noticed some shifts recently — assignments, meetings — and I want to understand what's actually going on. Not to defend myself. To get clarity so I can plan."*
*"Would you tell me honestly: is my continued employment here at risk?"*
*"If yes: what specifically would need to change? And what is a realistic timeline?"*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"I feel like I'm being marginalized."*
*"It seems like people don't appreciate my work."*
*"Am I in trouble?"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Sometimes the honest answer is that you are being managed out and there is nothing you can do about it. In that case, your best move is to leverage your remaining time to line up your next role, negotiate a reasonable exit package, and leave professionally. The clarity is the gift; the outcome may still be hard.

entries.title: Card #19: The Family Member Who Needs Serious Help

blocks.text: THE SITUATION

A close family member — parent, sibling, adult child — is in a downward spiral: addiction, mental health crisis, chronic financial mismanagement. They haven't asked for help. You are watching from a distance.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Cross your fingers. Give unsolicited advice they ignore. Or: intervene without professional understanding of what actually helps.
WHY IT FAILS

Waiting rarely produces spontaneous improvement in these situations. Unsolicited advice from family members is emotionally charged and often produces defensive responses rather than change. Untrained intervention can make things worse — for example, 'tough love' has been shown by research to be counterproductive in some addiction contexts.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE

Learn what actually works for this specific situation before you act. There are researched approaches (Motivational Interviewing, CRAFT for addiction, etc.) and professionals who can advise family members. Then act — but from an informed position.
WORDS TO USE
*"I love you and I'm worried about you. I don't want to pretend I haven't noticed. Can we talk about what's going on, when you're ready?"*
*"I'm not asking you to have an answer. I just want you to know I'm here, and I'll listen."*
*"I've been reading about how families can be helpful in situations like this. Would you be open to me sharing what I've learned?"*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"You need to get help."*
*"Why won't you just [X]?"*
*"I've done everything I can for you."*
*"This is your problem."*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some situations require professional intervention regardless of family effort. If there is danger of harm to self or others, do not manage it as a family — engage emergency services or specialized professionals. Family love is essential AND insufficient in some cases. Know the difference.

entries.title: Card #20: The Discovery That a Long-Trusted Colleague Lied

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
You discover, through information that came to you incidentally, that a colleague you have trusted for years lied to you about something significant.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Confront them immediately in an emotional moment. Or: silently downgrade the relationship without ever discussing it. Or: tell mutual colleagues.
WHY IT FAILS

Immediate confrontation, driven by hurt, rarely produces the outcome you want. Silent downgrade wastes the relationship without giving them a chance to explain or apologize. Telling mutual colleagues turns a private matter public and often reflects poorly on you, not just them.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Cool down first. Then bring it up directly, with them, in private. Give them a chance to explain. Decide, based on what you learn, whether the relationship is repairable or not.
WORDS TO USE
*"I want to talk to you about something that's affecting how I feel about our working relationship. I found out that [specific thing]. That's different from what you told me. Help me understand."*
*"I'm not trying to prosecute this. I want to know what actually happened, and I want us to be honest about where we are."*
*"Whatever we decide about our relationship going forward, I need to know the truth first."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"How could you?!"*
*"I'll never trust you again."*
*"Everyone thinks…"*
*"I know what you did. [before verifying]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Sometimes the explanation is genuine — a misunderstanding, a moment of weakness now regretted, a context you didn't have. Sometimes it isn't — the lie is part of a pattern. Both outcomes require the conversation to happen. Only then can you decide.

entries.title: Card #21: The Client Who Ghosts After a Verbal Commitment

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
A prospective client verbally committed to a deal at the end of a great meeting. Two weeks later, they've stopped responding to emails.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Send progressively desperate follow-ups. Or: give up and mentally close the deal as lost. Or: assume they must be angry about something and try to guess what.
WHY IT FAILS

Escalating desperation reads as neediness and damages your negotiating position on this deal or any future one. Giving up abandons a real possibility that a simple recovery move would have resolved. Guessing at hidden anger creates paranoid dynamics that sometimes materialize.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE

Send ONE more well-crafted message, then MOVE ON publicly. The clean move: 'I've reached out a few times without hearing back. That's fine — timing is hard. I'm going to stop reaching out for now. If circumstances change, I'd love to hear from you.' Then actually stop.
WORDS TO USE

*"I wanted to close the loop rather than keep adding noise. It sounds like the timing may not be right on your end — no need to explain. If things shift, I'd be glad to pick this up again. In the meantime, wishing you well."*
*"No response needed."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"Just following up on my previous message…"*
*"Circling back in case my last email got missed…"*
*"Just wondering if you had a chance to consider…"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Sometimes clients come back weeks or months later — and the clean closure message is why they feel comfortable doing so. Sometimes they don't. Either outcome is fine. You have preserved your dignity and your negotiating stance for the next opportunity.

entries.title: Card #22: The Colleague Who Cries in a One-on-One

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
In a routine one-on-one with a direct report or colleague, they begin crying. It is not a small moment — real, sustained emotion.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Panic. Offer tissues awkwardly. Try to fix the underlying problem immediately. Or: continue the meeting as if nothing had happened.
WHY IT FAILS

Trying to fix an emotional moment intellectually misses what the person needs — usually acknowledgment and space. Continuing as if nothing happened denies the reality of what just occurred and damages the working relationship.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Acknowledge. Give space. Ask what they need. Follow up privately later.
WORDS TO USE
*"Take a moment. There's no rush."*
*"I appreciate you letting me see this. Do you want to keep talking, or would you like to reschedule so you can have some time?"*
*"Is there something specific I can do — either about what triggered this, or just as your manager/colleague?"*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"Please don't cry."*
*"Are you okay? [asked repeatedly]"*
*"Let's just move on."*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some people will be embarrassed later about having cried at work. Do not treat the moment as a big event when following up — just check in briefly and normally, without making the crying itself the topic. Their emotional reaction is theirs; your job is to make space for it without amplifying it.

entries.title: Card #23: The Promotion That Went to Someone Else

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
A role you interviewed for internally, and thought you were the strongest candidate for, went to a colleague. Your manager gives you the news with vague reassurance about 'growth opportunities.'
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Bitterly commiserate to peers. Reduce your effort. Or: pretend you didn't want it and act like nothing happened.
WHY IT FAILS
Bitterness compounds and is visible. Reduced effort confirms every doubt that led to the decision. Pretending you didn't want it damages your ability to advocate for yourself in the future.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Ask for a real debrief. Not defensive — genuinely asking. Learn what actually drove the decision. Then decide, with more information, what to do next.
WORDS TO USE

*"I want to have a real conversation about this decision — not to argue with it, but to understand it. What specifically about my candidacy came up short? What would need to be true for me to be the obvious choice next time?"*
*"I'd also like to hear honestly whether you see a path for me here in the medium term, or whether this decision means something about the longer-term fit."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"I can't believe you gave it to them."*
*"Was it because of [X]?"*
*"This is unfair."*
*"I don't understand. [as complaint rather than inquiry]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Sometimes the honest debrief reveals that you are not going to be promoted at this company — because of factors beyond your control, or because your growth path lies elsewhere. That is painful, and it is also useful information. Better to know than to invest another two years hoping.

entries.title: Card #24: The Time You Realize You Overcommitted

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
You said yes to too many things. Three weeks in, you cannot deliver everything you promised without quality suffering across the board.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Try to do everything anyway. Sacrifice sleep and quality. Hope no one notices. Or: silently drop the commitment that feels least important, without telling the person you committed to.
WHY IT FAILS
The 'do everything anyway' path leads to burnout and delivered mediocrity across the whole list. Silent dropping damages the trust of the specific person you promised.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Renegotiate proactively, with each stakeholder, before you fail. Sooner is dramatically better than later.
WORDS TO USE

*"I want to have an honest conversation. I committed to X, Y, and Z on similar timelines and I've realized that doing all three well isn't possible. I want to renegotiate WITH you rather than under-deliver on you."*
*"Here are the options I see: [specific alternatives — pushing the timeline, reducing scope, or reprioritizing]. What would work best for your side?"*
*"I apologize for not seeing this earlier."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"I might be running late on this…"*
*"Just so you know, there's a lot going on…"*
*"I'll get it done, don't worry. [when you can't]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some stakeholders will be more understanding than others. Some will lose trust in you either way. The renegotiation is not free — but it is dramatically cheaper than the alternative. Learn from the pattern: you overcommitted. What was the driver? Ambition? People-pleasing? A specific person's pressure? Fix that, or you'll do it again.

entries.title: Card #25: The Sudden Illness of a Team Member

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
One of your team members is hospitalized suddenly. You don't know how serious it is. Their work is in-progress and time-sensitive.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Immediately reassign all their work without consulting them or their family. Or: freeze and do nothing until you 'know more.'
WHY IT FAILS
Reassigning without consultation removes their agency and can feel like erasure. Freezing sacrifices the work that could be handled and leaves the team in limbo.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Reach out to the family with care. Cover the critical work quietly. Communicate to the team with respect for the person and the situation.
WORDS TO USE

*"[To family, if you can reach them:] I'm so sorry to hear about [name]. Please know that we're covering their work here and there is zero urgency from our side. Whatever you need from us, please let us know. When [name] is well enough, they can reach out — but not before."*

*"[To the team:] [Name] is in the hospital. I don't have more information and I want to respect their privacy. Here's how we're covering their in-progress work: [plan]. Please give the family space; if you want to send a note, please route it through me so we don't overwhelm."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"What's going to happen with their projects?"*
*"Send them lots of texts to cheer them up!"*
*"We need to talk about how to handle their workload."*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

If the illness is prolonged, at some point you will need to make longer-term arrangements. Do this in consultation with the person (if possible) and with HR guidance on any legal or benefits implications. Do not surprise them with major changes when they return.

entries.title: Card #26: The Interview Where You Didn't Prepare Enough

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
You are 10 minutes into an interview and realize you did not prepare adequately. You don't know a key fact about the company that they clearly expected you to know.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Pretend you know. Bluff. Or: apologize profusely and lose composure for the rest of the interview.
WHY IT FAILS
Bluffing is caught 90% of the time by experienced interviewers. Falling apart hurts every subsequent answer.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Acknowledge cleanly. Recover. Focus on what you do know and what genuine curiosity you bring.
WORDS TO USE

*"Honestly, I hadn't dug into that specific area before this conversation — I want to give you a real answer, not a guess. Could you tell me a bit about it? I'll come back to this in follow-up if it's a key area for the role."*
*"I want to focus on where I can add value — here's how I'd approach the kind of problem you described, even without full context on [X]."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"Yes, I know all about that. [when you don't]"*
*"Sorry, I'm not really familiar with that. [without recovery]"*
*"That wasn't in the materials they sent me."*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some interviewers value the honest admission more than a bluff — it demonstrates security and intellectual honesty. Some won't. If they don't, the mismatch is probably a signal that this wouldn't have been the right role anyway.

entries.title: Card #27: The Business Partner Who Wants Out

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
Your business co-founder or partner tells you they want to exit the business. You are financially and emotionally invested in continuing.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Try to talk them out of it. Or: agree immediately on their terms out of shock or fear.
WHY IT FAILS
Talking someone out of a considered decision rarely produces long-term commitment. Agreeing under shock produces terms you'll regret.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Get the full picture — what's driving the decision, what the timeline looks like, what a fair exit structure would be. Then negotiate deliberately.
WORDS TO USE
*"I hear you. Before we get into terms, help me understand what's driving this — because that affects everything about how we structure the exit."*
*"What's your ideal timeline? Six months? Twelve?"*
*"I want us to do this in a way that both of us look back on well. Can we take a week to each propose a structure separately, then compare?"*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"You can't just leave!"*
*"Fine, whatever you want."*
*"After everything I did for this…"*
*"So how much do you want? [immediately]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Sometimes the exit reveals underlying issues — with you, with the business, with the relationship — that you weren't aware of. Whether the exit happens or not, the conversation can be an opportunity to fix things you didn't know were broken. Do not treat it as pure crisis.

entries.title: Card #28: The Company That Is Slowly Dying

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
You work at a company whose trajectory is clearly declining. Leadership is in denial. Colleagues are leaving. You've been telling yourself it will recover.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Wait for it to become obvious to everyone. Or: leave in a panic when things collapse.
WHY IT FAILS
Waiting until the collapse is public means competing with all your colleagues for the same new roles at the same time. Panicking produces hasty decisions.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Recognize the pattern honestly. Begin a deliberate, unhurried job search while still performing well in your current role.
WORDS TO USE
*"[To yourself, honestly:] The signals I'm seeing are: [list]. The most likely trajectory is [X]. I don't have to be certain. But I want to be ready."*
*"[To your network:] I'm doing well at [current company] but I've decided to explore what else is out there. Would you be open to a coffee to hear what you're seeing in the market?"*
*"[To interviewers:] I've enjoyed my role at [current company]. I'm exploring what's next because [honest, non-catastrophic framing]."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"I have to get out of there before it collapses."*
*"[to interviewers] The company is falling apart."*
*"[to yourself] It'll probably turn around."*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

You may be wrong about the trajectory. Companies sometimes recover from apparent decline. But quietly exploring options costs almost nothing and preserves optionality. The worst case of 'looking around and staying' is dramatically better than the worst case of 'staying without looking.'

entries.title: Card #29: The Ex-Colleague Who Slanders You

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
A former colleague — someone you had conflict with — is now speaking negatively about you in the industry. Others are telling you.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Respond publicly. Get into an argument with them in shared professional spaces. Or: try to manipulate others into defending you.
WHY IT FAILS
Public arguments amplify the slander to people who hadn't heard it. Attempting to organize a defense reads as insecure and often produces the opposite of the intended effect.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE

Do nothing publicly. Continue to demonstrate the opposite of whatever they're saying, through your actual work and behavior. Reach out privately to the most important 3-4 relationships in your network with honest context.
WORDS TO USE

*"[To close professional friends:] I want to give you the context you haven't heard, in case it comes up. [Brief, factual account.] I don't need you to do anything — I just want you to have the full picture."*

*"[To the ex-colleague, if a real conversation seems possible:] I've heard from a few people that you've been talking about our history. I'd rather hear directly from you than from them. Would you be open to a call?"*
*"[To yourself:] Reputation is built over decades. Individual slanders rarely define it. Keep doing the work."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"Have you heard what [X] is saying about me?"*
*"I need to set the record straight."*
*"Let me tell you what really happened…"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Occasionally, the slander is severe enough that it materially affects specific opportunities. In that case: consult a professional (lawyer, reputation-management advisor). Do not respond in public. Do not engage the ex-colleague on public channels. These situations get worse when the target responds.

entries.title: Card #30: The Mentor Who Betrays a Confidence

blocks.text: THE SITUATION
You told a trusted mentor something in confidence. You discover, through a specific incident, that they shared it — probably not maliciously, but definitely.
WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO
Confront them furiously. Cut ties without a word. Or: pretend it didn't happen and hope they wouldn't do it again.
WHY IT FAILS
Confrontation-in-anger burns a relationship that was probably valuable in ways beyond this incident. Silent cutoff denies you information about what really happened. Pretending sets up a recurrence.
THE RESOURCEFUL RESPONSE
Address it directly, in private, calmly. Assess based on their response whether the relationship survives.
WORDS TO USE

*"I want to tell you something that's affected how I feel about our relationship. I found out that [X] came up in your conversation with [Y]. I had shared that with you in confidence. I'm not looking for you to be perfect — I want to understand what happened."*
*"Based on what you tell me, I'm going to decide what to bring to you in the future."*
WORDS TO AVOID
*"How could you?"*
*"I'll never trust you again."*
*"I heard from [Y] that… [before verifying with the mentor]"*
WHAT CAN STILL GO WRONG

Some mentors will apologize genuinely, and the relationship can continue with adjusted expectations. Some will minimize or blame you for bringing it up. The latter is diagnostic — the mentor relationship has an important limit. Trust what you see.
**· CLOSING THE SUPPLEMENTS ·**

Eight Boss Fight second passes and fifteen more situation cards. Together with the material in the main text, they cover most of the interpersonal, professional, and moral moments that will define a modern working life.

You will not remember every card. That is fine. What matters is that you return to them when a specific situation matches — before you act, not after. The book becomes valuable in exactly this way: as the reference you consult on Tuesday morning before the hard call.

Every situation you handle well shapes the person you become. Every situation you handle badly does too. The difference is not that capable people never handle situations badly. The difference is that they return to think about what they would do differently — and, over years, become the person you become by that returning.
REMEMBER THIS
*“Return to the book. The book is a friend that improves with re-reading.”*
